result_text:
**The data can't tell us the effect of B, and it can't say whether B reaches your 1-point threshold.** Assignment was random, but 200 of B's 1,000 visitors have no recorded outcome, and A has none missing.

| Estimate for B minus A | Difference | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Complete case (800 known B outcomes: 96/800 = 12.0%, against A's 100/1000 = 10.0%) | +2.0 pp | −0.9 to +4.9 pp |
| Worst case (all 200 missing did not sign up: 9.6%) | −0.4 pp | −3.0 to +2.2 pp |
| Best case (all 200 missing signed up: 29.6%) | +19.6 pp | +16.2 to +23.0 pp |

- **Complete case:** The +2.0 pp point estimate is above 1 pp, but its interval includes zero and negative values. It also assumes the missing outcomes are unrelated to signup, and nothing in the data supports that.
- **Worst and best case:** The plausible range, allowing for the missing outcomes and for sampling noise, runs from about −3 pp to +23 pp. That range contains zero and the 1 pp threshold, so neither "B is better by at least 1 pp" nor "B is no better" follows.
- **Why the missing outcomes matter:** Randomization balances who was assigned to each page, but not who ended up with a missing outcome. Only B has missing outcomes, so the cause may be tied to the page itself, for example a tracking or redirect problem. If so, the complete-case comparison could be biased in either direction, and I can't tell which.

To resolve it, find out why 200 B visitors have no outcome. If those outcomes were lost at random, the complete-case estimate (+2 pp, still uncertain) becomes defensible. Better still, recover the outcomes themselves.

The working record is in `work/estimation_record.md`. The estimates are Wald intervals computed by hand, and I didn't run any other checks.
